content.title: About
content.content: Cereal, O's, multigrain are whole‑grain ring‑shaped flakes enriched with vitamins and minerals. They are made from a blend of wheat, oats, rice and corn, providing a balanced mix of carbohydrates, fiber and protein. The flakes have a light crunchy texture and a mild aroma, perfect for a breakfast with milk or yogurt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend includes five different grains, giving higher nutritional value than single‑grain cereals.
The flakes are fortified with B‑vitamins, iron and zinc to support energy metabolism and immunity.
The ring shape was designed for easy portion control and even milk absorption.
The product contains no artificial colors or flavors.
Packaging is made from recyclable material and can be reused.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: The whole‑grain blend provides a high amount of fiber, which aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs release energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B6 and folate support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Fortified with minerals
items.content: Iron, zinc and magnesium contribute to immune health, blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Added sugar content is minimal, making the cereal suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: People allergic to wheat, oats or other grains may experience reactions.

items.title: Contains gluten
items.content: Not suitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic impact with sweeteners
items.content: Adding honey, syrup or other sweeteners can raise the glycemic index.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour milk, kefir or a plant‑based drink over the flakes and let them sit for 2–3 minutes. They can also be mixed into yogurt, smoothies, used in baking, or as a crunchy topping for fruit salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. For longer shelf life, keep in the refrigerator to preserve crunchiness and prevent fat oxidation.

chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-sauteed-.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, sautéed, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs are dark meat cuts rich in protein and nutrients. When sautéed without the skin, most of the excess fat drips away, making the dish lower in calories while still flavorful and juicy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark chicken meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
In traditional Russian cuisine, chicken legs are often pan‑fried with onions and spices.
Cooking without skin lets the rendered fat collect in the pan, allowing better control of calorie intake.
Thighs stay tender during long‑slow cooking, which is why they are popular in stews.
In many countries, chicken drumsticks are served with barbecue sauce for a sweet‑tangy flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Dark meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Chicken meat contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: High sodium if salted heavily
items.content: Excess salt can raise blood pressure, so season moderately.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to chicken proteins and may experience reactions.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Chicken contains purines, which can exacerbate gout in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté the pieces over medium heat after seasoning with salt, pepper, garlic and your favorite herbs. Serve with roasted vegetables, mashed potatoes or whole‑grain rice. Leftovers keep for up to 3 days in the fridge and can be added to salads, soups or wraps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw pieces in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 2 days. Cooked portions can be refrigerated for 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags at –18 °C (0 °F) for up to 3 months.

fish-whiting-baked-or-broiled-coated.title: Fish, whiting, baked or broiled, coated

content.title: About
content.content: Whiting is a lean white fish from the cod family, commonly prepared baked or broiled after being coated. The cooking method keeps the flesh moist while the coating adds a crisp texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whiting inhabits coastal waters of the Atlantic and North Sea.
In the United States it is often marketed as a low‑cost source of protein.
Coatings may include breadcrumbs, flour, herbs, and sometimes grated Parmesan.
Baking at 180‑200 °C retains most of the fish’s nutrients.
Whiting cooks quickly—usually 10‑15 minutes in the oven.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 18 g of complete protein, essential for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with fatty fish, whiting contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and B6, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Whiting is a source of selenium, iodine, and phosphorus, important for thyroid health and bones.

items.title: Moderate omega‑3
items.content: Although lower than oily fish, it still contributes omega‑3 fatty acids that benefit heart health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including whiting.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Like other marine fish, whiting can contain trace amounts of mercury or cadmium; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Sodium in coating
items.content: Prepared breadcrumb mixes often contain added salt; watch sodium intake if needed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coat fillets with a mixture of breadcrumbs, herbs, and a drizzle of olive oil, then bake or broil until golden. It can also be pan‑fried quickly. Serve with lemon wedges, fresh herbs, and a side of vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh fillets should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped tightly, and used within 2 days. Frozen fillets store up to 3 months at –18 °C. Thaw frozen fish in the fridge before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Milk shake with malt is a refreshing beverage made from milk, ice cream, malt flavoring, and sometimes a splash of cream. The malt gives it a sweet, slightly caramel-like taste reminiscent of beer notes, but without any alcohol.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The malt used in the shake is derived from sprouted barley that is dried and roasted.
The first malt‑flavored milk shake appeared in the United States in the 1960s as a fast‑food menu item.
Malt aroma often evokes childhood memories of the Soviet‑era “milk bar” ice creams.
The shake can be served cold or warm by substituting hot milk for ice.
Malt extract contains small amounts of B‑vitamins retained from the grain.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The milk base provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Milk and ice cream supply a complete set of amino acids that support muscle recovery.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Malt extract retains modest levels of vitamins B1, B2 and niacin, aiding energy metabolism.

items.title: Mood‑boosting
items.content: The sweet taste and malt aroma can stimulate serotonin production, helping improve mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The shake often contains a lot of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain if consumed frequently.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should use lactose‑free milk or plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Allergy to milk or dairy proteins makes the shake unsuitable for some individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Added ice cream and cream make the drink calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the milk shake with malt in tall glasses, topped with whipped cream and a sprinkle of ground malt or cinnamon. It can be sipped through a straw or used as a sauce for desserts such as pancakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The shake is best enjoyed immediately. If you need to store it, keep it refrigerated in a sealed container for no more than 2‑3 hours to prevent cream separation.

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn chips are crunchy snacks made from whole popcorn kernels that are toasted until golden and lightly salted. They have a light, airy flavor and a distinctive crunch that resembles traditional popcorn but in a thin chip form.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn chips are produced from whole popcorn kernels, not from corn starch.
Compared with regular potato chips, they contain less fat because popcorn is naturally light.
They are popular in vegetarian and vegan diets as they contain no animal ingredients.
Many flavor variations exist, but the plain version preserves the natural popcorn taste.
Popcorn is the only type of corn that “pops” when heated, creating an airy structure.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Popcorn chips usually contain less fat than traditional potato chips, making them a lighter snack option.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Whole popcorn kernels are rich in dietary fiber, which supports digestive health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Popcorn has a lower glycemic index compared with many other grain‑based snacks, helping to stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Popcorn contains polyphenols that have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Popcorn chips are made from corn, which is naturally gluten‑free, suitable for gluten‑free diets.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn, making popcorn chips unsafe for them.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although lightly salted, people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite lower fat, popcorn chips still contain calories and should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: The crunchy texture can pose a choking risk for young children; serve under supervision.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popcorn chips can be enjoyed straight from the bag, added to salads, used as a crunchy base for dips, or mixed with dried fruit and nuts for a snack blend.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn chips in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to maintain crunch and prevent staleness.

seafood-garden-salad-with-seafood-lettuc.title: Seafood Garden Salad with Seafood, Lettuce, and Vegetables (no tomato, no carrot)

content.title: About
content.content: Seafood Garden Salad is a light dish made of fresh seafood (shrimp, mussels, calamari), crisp lettuce, cucumber, bell pepper, radish and green onion. It is prepared without tomatoes or carrots and without any dressing to let the natural flavors shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Seafood is a rich source of omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health.
Lettuce contains over 90 % water, making the salad refreshing and low‑calorie.
Excluding tomatoes reduces acidity, which can be beneficial for people with reflux.
Red bell pepper is one of the highest‑vitamin C vegetables available.
The dish is often featured in health‑focused restaurants as a “clean” option without sauces.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Seafood provides complete protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s help lower triglycerides, reduce inflammation, and support brain function.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Lettuce, cucumber and bell pepper supply vitamin C, vitamin K, potassium and folate.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: No dressing and no high‑calorie ingredients make this salad ideal for weight management.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high water content of the vegetables contributes to proper hydration.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels or calamari; caution is advised.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the seafood is pre‑salted, sodium levels can be high; choose fresh or well‑rinsed options.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Raw seafood can harbor pathogens; use only high‑quality, properly handled products.

items.title: Nutrient interactions
items.content: People on anticoagulants should monitor vitamin K intake from lettuce.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad immediately after assembly to keep the textures crisp. A squeeze of lemon or fresh herbs can be added for extra brightness, but avoid dressings that mask the seafood’s natural taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad at room temperature for no more than 2 hours. If needed, refrigerate in a sealed container, but it is best enjoyed right away to prevent the lettuce from wilting.
